Good afternoon, Chair Mansfield, Vice Chair Estreffi, members of the board, and Dr. Spence. I am happy to welcome Naomi Hunter of the National School Public Relations Association to present the findings of our communications audit. She is the INSPRA Communications Surveys Manager and was the lead auditor for LCPS.

Naomi, thank you for being here. Thank you so much, Natalie, Dr. Spence, and the board. It's a pleasure to be here. It's been a pleasure working on the communications audit for your division. First, I want to tell you just what we're going to do tonight. You all have a copy of the report, so this is going to be a high-level presentation.

We'll summarize the points, and then I'll take questions at the end. I'm going to give you the overall goal of an audit, what the audit process involved. We'll review top-line key findings, including the strengths and opportunities for your division, and I'll also just highlight some of the recommendations and action steps that we are recommending and considerations for the division as you begin to implement.

So I was the lead auditor, as Natalie said. However, there was a whole team behind me, and I just want to take a minute and give them credit, especially my co-auditor, Steve Mulvannon, who was here with me in December and co-wrote the report with me.

We also had two audit assistants who came and were participating in all the focus groups, listening, taking notes. And then we have an editing team back at the office, including Susan Downing and Melissa Bram, who is the associate director of the National School of Public Relations Association.
The goal of the audit was threefold. One, we wanted to seek data, opinion, and perceptions and assess the effectiveness and management of public relations and marketing in your district.

We also provide customized recommendations on strategies and best practices to help you go to the next level in your communication. One thing I always like to say when I'm presenting an audit to a board is that this audit really represents a snapshot in time.

It's going to somewhat reflect whatever was going on in the division at the time that we did the focus groups and the survey. But we also have found over years of doing many, many of these audits that whatever conditions were present at that time, the audit does reflect a general, it's going to give you a really good general read of the situation in relation to communication in your division.
We start the audit process with a review of your materials, and I will compliment Natalie and Joan and the team for providing us with a really comprehensive set of materials.

We look at your publications, your policies, campaigns you've done, media coverage. Then we do the scope survey, which I'll talk about in the next slide. And then we come in and do the focus groups. So by the time we get here, we already know quite a lot about the division.
And in this particular case, we really had a lot of material to work with. We conducted what we call the SCOPE Survey, which is the School Communications Performance Evaluation.
It was conducted from November 28th to December 15th of 2023. We set goals when we do a SCOPE Survey. We set target goals that we know tell us that the survey is going to be reliable.

And the goal is to get a margin of error of 5%. And that is all calculated based on formulas. And I want you to know that LCPS had the lowest margin of error, the highest participation of any scope survey I've conducted.

And I've conducted 35 of them in the last year and a half. So rest assured that you had really very high participation and the results are reliable. We conducted, I believe it was 20 focus groups and interviews during the week that we were here.

We talked to parents, we talked to students, we talked to teachers, department leaders, professional staff. We went to your transportation department and interviewed your transportation team, as well as doing interviews with Dr. Spence, with Natalie, with Joan, and with several of you on the board.

And those were really helpful in providing qualitative information. So whereas the scope survey provides us with the quantitative data, the focus groups help us to dig deep and probe and see what might be behind some of the numbers.

I will not be going over every finding. As I said, you do have an extensive report, but I do want to highlight just a couple of them. We always ask overall perception of a division or district when we're doing the scope survey and part of the reason for this is to get a read on it relates to branding and marketing what is the perception out there in the community of your division and lcps was just about at the national average pretty close 60 of parents and employees rate the division as excellent or above

average but i do want to point out that when compared to a set of large districts of 50 000 Students enrolled or more you actually exceeded the national average on this measure and then an overall satisfaction with communication 50% of your parents and 40% of employees rated satisfaction with communication as excellent or above average and again You were pretty close to the national average and at the national average for a subset of large school districts

We were very impressed in the interviews we did at the professional backgrounds, expertise of the staff. And last I'll just say that you have so much to work with. We heard a prevailing theme throughout the audit of people wanting to hear more good news stories.

And the great thing is you have a lot of good stories to tell. So we consider that a strength. As far as areas of challenge, because of your location near Washington, D.C., you do get heightened media attention.

We noted with some focus groups and in the scope data a perceived lack of transparency. And some of that we believe comes from the rapid growth of the division from being a relatively smaller division 20 or 30 years ago to the size that you are today and things haven't necessarily kept up and that sometimes gets in the way of releasing information in the most effective way.

We also noted that there's a lot of amazing family engagement efforts going on throughout the division but they're not centralized. So one group might be doing one thing, another group might be doing another thing. We found also internally some lack of clarity around communicating messages, not so much from the communications office out but, you know, from department to department.

And so when we go through the recommendations, I'll talk about some of our recommendations for that. And the last area of challenge that I'll highlight is just that the community at large doesn't necessarily have all the information they need to know the great things going on.

And one thing we learned is that your division has a higher than normal percentage of employees, community members who are affiliated, either because their children are enrolled or they work here. But still, there is a group out there that is more disconnected.

Just some top-level observations before I dive into our recommendations. The high-profile media coverage, as we listened to employees and even parents talk, it seems to have created, it's eroded trust and confidence out in the community, but it's also created a bit of an atmosphere of caution among staff, among people being fearful that something they say might be misinterpreted, and we'll talk about that as we go in, and also just fear of violating privacy and where are those lines.

There are many social and cultural divides right now that are amplifying some of this and that, I want to be clear, is not just LCPS. This is, I think, the eighth audit I've conducted in the last two years and in every single one this has come up.

So it's not only you but it is something that's affecting you. As I alluded to in the last slide, we do see opportunities for the infrastructure to change and adapt to the current size of your division. And we also note that as the division has grown, that has widened the array of perspectives and points of view, and that is both a challenge and an opportunity.

You do have that opportunity to listen and bring in new ideas and innovation. And last and most importantly, we really noted that you are at a turning point in your communication efforts. And that's something that we also heard over and over again in the focus groups.

Many people noted with the new board, new superintendent, there's really an opportunity to take things to the next level. I'm going to devote one slide to each of these recommendations. And I won't talk in great detail on each slide.

I'm going to highlight one or two things that I think would be important for you to know because I want to make sure that I leave some time at the end for your questions. One is to expand the current strategic communications plan into a more comprehensive plan.

This is something that would have been difficult to do prior to having the results of the Scope Survey. We were very impressed that your team has a detailed plan with many tactics already spelled out. So they're ahead of many districts that you are ahead of many divisions that we audit.
But what we are recommending now is to take that existing plan and compare it against the findings of the audit and make it more strategic so that it can support your overall division goals.

Recommendation two. I will also just say, as I said, I'm not going to talk about every point, but in the report we do put in a lot of links to work being done by other districts and divisions around the country that have tackled similar things.

So there's a whole wealth of resources for Natalie and the team to draw on. As I mentioned just a minute ago, many people said to us, we have an opportunity to rebuild trust and confidence after a difficult time.

And we believe that's true. And so our recommendation here is we really laud Dr. Spence for doing that extensive listening tour throughout the school year. I know that's a big investment of time for a superintendent. and we encourage continuing that in whatever way works.

You know, maybe it's doing some things off-site at a public setting or doing some virtual engagement opportunities, but keep that up because we think it's going to make a big difference. We're also recommending forming a community trust-building committee, and Natalie and I were chatting about this just the other day, and that's something you can use your existing committees to leverage, your superintendent advisory groups and Natalie will be working with you as a board to determine the best way to do this but the idea of that group is to help you understand how things are being perceived out in the community so that

there's not there aren't things that are being talked about that you're not aware of it's just a way to keep a pulse on the community another point that I I want to make, that's actually not in the slide here, but it's often missed that trust and confidence are really closely connected to student performance, and the reason I want to highlight that a little bit is when you have the trust of your community, which is going to happen through the tactics that are recommended here, you're going to get more

support for those strategies and things that you want to do to help students and not be distracted by things that are outside of a focus on students and academics so I just wanted to make sure that I made that connection for you recommendation three is to improve the communication infrastructure I will say it's important to me to say that everybody here was already aware of the need to do that so it's not like when I came back and said that to Natalie or Dr. Spence that they were surprised but what I hope that our report does is provide some practical

tangible ways for that to happen. And a lot of it is just around clarifying roles, making sure that you're following the same processes, and also streamlining the number of tools. It seemed to us that there was confusion around that.
And so there are some specific ideas for doing some streamlining. Recommendation four is to combat misinformation and disinformation. Well that's a really big one and it's really hard to do.

But our recommendation is that you have a very deliberate effort to monitor emerging issues and we have some ideas in the report for how that might occur. To make sure that any time the Board is considering something that might be a hot button or might be misunderstood that there's always fact sheets that help frame that conversation and make sure that people have accurate information.

And education to the community so that your stakeholders understand that sometimes information gets out that's not true. And sometimes merely telling someone that facts that are released by non-district sources might be true.
It may just be a mistake, but when people know, then they're more careful and more considered about what they believe.

Recommendation five has to do with a more proactive media relations plan. One thing that you may not be aware of is that media is a higher valued source in LCPS than in most of the other divisions or districts that I have audited.

In fact, in the report I include a data point on that, that 32% of your stakeholders use local media as a source to learn about your district. But I would say of the last five districts that I audited prior to LCPS, that ranged from 13 to 22 percent.

So it's more important here than in other school systems for you to ensure that you're really in close contact with the media and providing them with a steady stream of information. One of the things that we're recommending is media relations training and that is primarily to build confidence because there's a real link between hesitancy.

Sometimes hesitancy can get in the way of transparency. So we know that you all want to tell the truth and get it out there. And we are recommending that everybody has some practice and some training so they can do that with confidence. Oops, sorry.

Recommendation six is strengthening the two-way communications culture. I talked a little bit earlier about family engagement and the decentralized nature of what we saw here. And that's the main thing that I want to emphasize in this slide.

There are many things you can do to strengthen two-way communications, but having a very deliberate effort of family engagement is probably one of the most important ones. And we learned about the face group and what great work they're doing.

And so one of our recommendations is to really use a lot of their work as a model, but to centralize all those efforts to map out all of the different groups in the division that are addressing family engagement and make sure that they're coordinated and leveraged with each other so that you're maximizing your efforts.

The other thing is transparency around the release of this report. And I know that's already planned, but, you know, we always hear, and again, this is not only LCPS. I hear this from other school systems as well, but people sometimes feel like they take surveys and they never hear the results of them.

So it's really important to let your constituents know that you've made this effort and you're investing in improving communication and that they can see the work and the recommendations that were done. And last but not least, we're recommending tactics to engage those local residents who aren't directly affiliated with your district already.

And I know that, for example, Natalie told me that she already is planning some inserts in the local papers. So this is some of the work that's already underway, which is a great segue for you to talk about some of what you're doing.

Natalie has a great team. You have a great comms department. But in the end, everybody who has contact with any member of the public is a communicator.
